text: The bread is out of the oven and the kitchen window has fogged over from the inside. I turn the radio down until it is mostly murmur and lean against the counter with the loaf cooling beside me. There is nowhere I need to be for the rest of the evening.

The dog has put his head on my foot and gone to sleep, and I am not going to move it. Down the street the neighbors' sprinkler ticks back and forth across their lawn. I sip what is left of my iced tea and watch the light go out of the sky.

The last sock has found its match and the stacks of laundry sit square on the bed. Late sun comes across the quilt and lands on my hands. I smooth the top towel once more than it needs and leave the pile where it is.

My son is asleep in the back seat with sand still on his legs and the beach towel wadded under his cheek. I drive the slow way home with the windows down two inches. Every few minutes I check the mirror just to see him breathing.

I have watered the whole garden and the tomato vines hang heavy against their stakes. The soil under my fingernails will take a scrub brush to get out. I sit on the overturned bucket and let the hose drip onto my boots.

The Sunday paper is spread across the table in sections and my second cup of coffee is still hot. The calendar on the fridge shows nothing until Tuesday. I fold the crossword back and settle deeper into the chair.

The hallway is painted and the rollers are soaking in the sink. I stand at one end and look down the length of it with the overhead light on. The color came out exactly the way it looked on the little card.

An hour has gone by on the phone with my oldest friend and I have refilled the kettle twice. Her voice sounds the same as it did when we were nineteen. I pull my feet up under me on the couch and let her finish the story.

Rain runs down the glass and the cat has arranged herself along the windowsill with her tail over her nose. My book is open on my knee at a page I have read twice without minding. The radiator ticks and settles.

The sauce tastes the way it did in my grandmother's kitchen, which has never happened before. I stand over the pot with the wooden spoon and take one more taste to be sure. Then I turn the flame down low and set the table for two.

The grocery bags cut a little into my fingers on the walk home, and from the corner I can see our apartment lights already on. Somebody is moving around in the kitchen. I shift the bags to one hand and dig for my keys without hurrying.

My legs are still humming from the ride and my shoes are off on the front step beside me. The bike leans against the railing with mud dried on its frame. I drink the whole bottle of water in one long pull and sit a while longer.

The first fire of the season is going in the woodstove and the split logs are stacked to the window ledge. I hold my palms out toward the glass door until they are almost too warm. The house smells like smoke and oranges.

She falls asleep in the middle of the page about the bear, her hand still on the picture. I keep reading in a whisper for another minute anyway. When I close the book I leave the lamp on and sit on the edge of the bed.

The fridge is full for the first time in two weeks, with the milk in the door and the vegetables washed and in their drawer. I stand with the door open longer than I should, just looking. Then I close it and wipe the handle with my sleeve.

The bedroom door has squeaked for three years and now it swings shut without a sound. I open it and close it twice more to be sure. The little can of oil goes back under the sink with its cap on tight.

I lean in the kitchen doorway and watch him chop onions with the knife I sharpened last weekend. He hums something I half recognize and does not know I am there yet. The pan is already warming on the back burner.
My feet hang off the end of the dock into water that is colder than the air. The boat knocks softly against its bumpers behind me. A dragonfly lands on my knee, considers it, and goes.

The monthly numbers come out with a little room to spare, which they have not done since spring. I write the total at the bottom of the page and underline it once. The pen goes back in the mug and I stretch my arms over my head.

I press the last tulip bulb into the cold ground and pat the soil over it with the flat of my hand. There are forty of them under here now, pointed end up, waiting for April. I wipe my hands on my jeans and look at the empty bed.

The rows add up under my needles while the television murmurs about weather somewhere else. The scarf is long enough now to reach my knees when I hold it up. I count the stitches once more and keep going.

Rain streaks the coffee shop window and steam rises off the cup in front of me. I have three clues left in the crossword and no plans for the afternoon. The woman at the next table laughs at something in her book.
The hammock holds me between two trunks and the leaves above shift light across my face. Somewhere a lawnmower starts and stops. I let one arm hang down until my fingertips brush the grass.

Half the sky is done, a thousand pieces of nearly the same blue, and the kitchen table has been covered for a week. I find the one with the wisp of cloud and press it in. My tea has gone cold and I drink it anyway.

The sheets are fresh from the line and I am clean from the shower, and it is not even nine o'clock. I slide in and pull the blanket up to my chin. The window is open a crack and the crickets are at it.
We walk the loop after dinner as the porch lights come on one by one along the block. My hand is in her coat pocket with hers. Neither of us says much and neither of us needs to.

The kids have pulled every cushion off the couch and built something with a tunnel and two rooms. I sit on the bare frame with my coffee and watch them negotiate the roof. Nobody has asked me for anything in twenty minutes.

The chain is oiled and the brakes grab clean and I take the bike once around the block to be sure. It shifts through every gear without a click. I roll it back into the garage and hang it on its hooks.

My mother and I shell peas on the back step with the colander between us. Her thumbnail splits each pod the same way it always has. The pile of empty shells grows beside her slipper and the pods ping into the bowl.

The envelope is addressed in my old teacher's handwriting, the same slant as on my report cards. I read the letter twice standing in the hall and then once more sitting down. I prop it against the sugar bowl where I will see it tomorrow.
Rain hammers the tin roof of the cabin and the cards are dealt for another hand. The woodstove has the room warm enough for socks and no shoes. My brother shuffles badly and nobody points it out.

The dog comes home from the groomer smelling of something floral and sits in the patch of sun on the kitchen floor. I sit down next to her with my back against the cabinet. We stay there until the sun moves.
The bakery bag is warm against my chest on the walk back and the whole street smells of it. I tear off the end of one roll before I reach the corner. Saturday has barely started.
The clay finally centers on the wheel after six weeks of wobbling, and a bowl rises between my hands almost on its own. I slow the wheel and let it spin to a stop. My forearms are gray to the elbow.
Nothing has taken the bait since dawn and the thermos is half empty. Mist lifts off the pond in slow sheets. I recast toward the reeds because the motion is reason enough.

Everyone is at the table at once, plates going around, someone laughing in the next room over a photo. I pass the potatoes to my left and take the bread from my right. The chair creaks under me the way it has for years.
The tank is clean and the fish are circling the fresh water in slow figure eights. I dry my arms and sit on the floor with my chin on the edge of the stand. The filter hums back up to speed.
Smoke from the grill drifts over the lawn chairs and a ballgame plays from a radio on the porch rail. I turn the corn and let the lid drop. Somebody hands me a cold can without my asking.

Fields slide past the train window in long green bands and my sandwich is still wrapped in foil on the tray. I have a window seat and three hours to go. I unwrap one corner and watch a barn come and go.
The button is back on the coat, the thread knotted twice and snipped. I try it through the buttonhole and it holds. The needle goes back into the little tomato cushion with the others.
The ladder is steady against the apple tree and the bucket at my hip is filling faster than I expected. I twist each one until the stem gives. Below me my daughter is eating more than she is picking.
The watercolor bleeds exactly where I let it, the wash of sky running down into the paper. I rinse the brush and lean back from the balcony table. The afternoon has gotten away from me and I let it.
The walk is shoveled and the bath is as hot as I can stand it. I sink down until the water closes over my shoulders. Through the little window I can see it has started snowing again.

Snow is coming down under the streetlight in the kind of flakes that take their time. I watch from the kitchen with the lights off and a mug in both hands. The plow has not come yet and the street is one smooth white sheet.
The campfire has burned down to the stage where the marshmallows go on, and three small faces lean in toward the coals. I hold my stick low and turn it slowly. Sparks go up and out over the lake.

The guests are gone and the dishwasher is humming through its first cycle. I wipe down the counters in long slow passes and put the last glass in the cabinet. The house holds the sound of the evening a little while longer.

The last box is unpacked and flattened and the books are on their shelves in roughly the right order. I sit on the floor in the middle of the room with my back against the couch. Out the new window there is a tree I had not noticed.
The barber lays the hot towel over my face and the shop goes dim and muffled. Scissors click somewhere to my left. I let my shoulders drop against the chair and stop keeping track of time.
Bubbles rise through the pancake batter and I wait for the edges to go dry before I flip. The kids are still in pajamas arguing about syrup. The stack on the plate is getting tall enough to lean.
I lie on the grass with my hands behind my head while my nephew names the clouds. That one is a dog, that one is also a dog. The ground is warm through my shirt.

The dogs run wide loops across the wet grass of the park and come back muddy to the shins. I stand with the other owners holding a leash I do not need yet. The coffee in my cup is the first of the day.

My father holds the board while I drive the nails, the way he used to hold it for his father. The fence line straightens post by post down the field. My pocket is heavy with the nails we have not used.
I close the cover of the novel and keep my hand flat on it for a moment. Eight hundred pages and the ending landed where it should. The couch cushion has my shape pressed into it.

The peach from the market stall is so ripe the juice runs down my wrist before I can catch it. I eat it standing in the shade of the awning. The farmer hands me a napkin and does not charge me for the second one.

My niece tosses bread to the ducks in handfuls too big for them and the ducks do not mind. I hold the back of her jacket so she does not follow them in. The pond is flat and the morning is going nowhere fast.

Everyone has left the office and my desk is cleared down to the lamp and one folder. The building ticks as it cools. I finish the last line of the report and sit for a minute before I reach for my coat.

The bug is somewhere in the parser and I am following it down one function at a time, reading faster than I can think about reading. My hands move between the keyboard and the trackpad without my telling them to. When I look up the window has gone dark and the office is empty.

The dough has reached the point where it pushes back against the heel of my hand, and I fold and turn and fold again in a rhythm I stopped counting a while ago. Flour dusts the floor around my feet. The timer went off at some point and I have no idea when.

The knife in my hand finds the grain of the wood and a long curl lifts away from the spoon's bowl. I turn the blank and go again, the shavings piling up on my apron. The porch light is on and I do not remember it coming on.

Solder flows into the joint the instant the iron touches it and I am already reaching for the next lead. The board is half populated and my eyes have stopped leaving the magnifier. Somewhere behind me my phone has buzzed three or four times.

The position on the board has opened up and I can see four moves down two different lines at once. My opponent's clock is running but I am not looking at it. I move the knight and my hand is back in my lap before the piece settles.

The wall is nothing but the next hold and the one after that, chalk on my fingers, my hip turning in before I decide to turn it. The rope tugs when my partner takes slack and I barely register it. My forearms will tell me later how long this took.

The drum pattern has locked in with the bass line and my hands are doing a thing my brain is only watching. Sweat runs into my collar. The rest of the band is somewhere out there and the song is carrying all of us.

The interview recording plays in my left ear and the words appear on the screen a half second behind, my fingers keeping pace without catching up. I have stopped hearing the voice as a voice. Forty minutes of audio are gone and the mug beside me is untouched.

The bead lays down even along the seam and I follow it with the torch at a speed my wrist has worked out on its own. Through the mask there is only the puddle and the edge of the metal. When I flip the visor up the shop is quiet and the other bay is dark.

The essay has found its argument somewhere in the third paragraph and now the sentences are arriving faster than I can type them. I stop fixing typos and just keep going. The cursor runs down the page and the coffee has a skin on it.

The French sentence resolves into English in my head before I have finished reading it, and the next one is already waiting. My pen does not lift from the paper between lines. I turn the page and the one after that and the library lights dim for closing.

The sander moves with the grain in long passes and the tabletop goes from rough to something my palm slides across without catching. Dust hangs in the garage light. I switch to the finer paper and keep going until the board tells me it is done.

The proof is unfolding on the whiteboard one line under the next and the marker squeaks as I go. I can see where it is heading two steps before I write it. My free hand is already erasing the scratch work from the corner.

My right hand reads the notes a bar ahead of my left and the page turns itself at the right moment. The piece is new to me and I am playing it anyway, mistakes and all, without stopping. The metronome has been off for a while and I have not missed it.

The shadow under her cheekbone comes up out of the charcoal and the rest of the face follows from it. I smudge with the side of my thumb and go back in with the edge of the stick. The model has shifted twice and I have adjusted without noticing.

Tile, mortar, spacer, tile, and the floor advances toward the far wall a row at a time. My knees are on the pad and my back has stopped complaining. The light through the bathroom window has moved from one wall to the other.

The thread wraps the hook in tight turns and the feather splays exactly where I want it. The vise holds steady and the lamp is the only light in the room. There are nine finished flies in the tray and I meant to tie two.

My daughter's hair divides into three and my fingers cross them over and under in the pattern my own mother used. The braid grows down her back while she reads. I reach for the elastic on my wrist without looking.

The blade drags across the stone at the same angle every stroke and the burr rolls over to the other side right on schedule. I flip it and count without numbers. The water in the tray has gone gray and I have not heard the dishwasher finish.

The hull of the model ship takes its planks one at a time, each one bent over steam and pinned while the glue sets. My tweezers know where the next pin is. The kitchen clock says something I decide not to read.

The cut lands on the beat and the next shot is already loaded in the timeline before I have thought about it. The scene is assembling itself under my hands. Outside the editing room someone says goodnight and I raise a hand without turning.

The brush loads with ink and the stroke comes down thick and lifts thin, the way the manual shows and the way my arm has only just learned. I move to the next character without rinsing. The sheet fills and I pull another from the stack.
The ball comes off the rim and I am already under it, the outlet pass leaving my hands before my feet are down. We run the floor and the score stops mattering. My lungs burn and I do not care.

The onions fall away from the knife in even half moons and the carrots follow and then the celery, the board filling faster than the pot can take it. I slide the pile in with the back of the blade and reach for the garlic. The kitchen has shrunk to the cutting board.

The kayak drops into the chute and my paddle finds the eddy line on its own, bracing and pulling in a sequence I could not describe afterward. The rock on the left goes by close. Then the water flattens and I am breathing again.

The seam feeds under the needle and my foot holds the pedal at a speed the fabric likes. I turn the corner, backstitch, and lift the presser foot in one motion. The dress is becoming a dress and the radio has been playing to nobody.

The old varnish comes off the chair leg in long ribbons under the scraper and the grain shows through for the first time in decades. I turn the leg and start the next face. My thumb is raw and I notice only when I stop.

The trail flags go in every twenty paces and the line of them bends around the big boulder exactly where the map in my head said it should. I pace, hammer, pace, hammer. The woods have gone orange with evening and I have another hundred yards in me.

The level has become a sequence of jumps my thumbs already know, and I am through the part that stopped me all week before I register it. The controller is warm. My brother says something from the doorway and I answer without hearing myself.

The paper folds along the crease and the crane's neck comes up out of the square, then the wings, each fold pressed with the back of my nail. I reach for another sheet before the first one is set down. The pile of birds on the desk is up to eleven.

The signatures stack under the needle and the thread pulls them tight against the tape, one, two, three, the kettle stitch catching each time. The spine is building up under my hands. The glue pot has gone tacky and I thin it without stopping.

The batter is folded to exactly the ribbon the recipe describes and I am piping rounds onto the sheet in a grid my hand keeps straight on its own. Tap the tray, slide it in, start the next. The oven timer and I have reached an understanding.

The idle smooths out as I turn the mixture screw a quarter at a time, listening with my whole head bent into the engine bay. My hands are black to the wrist. The radio in the next bay has been on for hours and I could not name one song.

The phrase of the dance comes together on the eighth try and then the next phrase arrives before I have finished the first. The mirror shows someone moving who is not deciding anything. The studio floor is slick under my feet and I go again.
The trail climbs and my feet find the roots and rocks a stride ahead of my eyes. My breath has settled into something I could keep up for an hour. The switchbacks go by and I stop counting them.

The wave stands up behind me and I am paddling, then up, then dropping down the face with my feet already where they need to be. The board tracks across the green wall. Everything is the next few feet of water.

The quilt blocks go together under the needle in the order the pattern laid out and the order my hands have memorized. Pin, sew, press, pin. The ironing board has been up since breakfast and it is nearly dinner.

The plaster goes on in arcs from the hawk and the trowel smooths it before it can set, one sweep leading into the next across the wall. My shoulder has found the rhythm and stopped asking questions. The wall is becoming one surface.

The shuttle passes through the shed and the beater comes forward and the cloth grows a thread at a time under my hands. My feet change the treadles without my counting. The loom's clack has become the only clock in the room.

The pipette tip finds each well in the plate in order and my eyes track the column while my thumb does the plunging. Ninety-six wells and the pattern does not break. The centrifuge hum fills the lab and I am alone in it.

The dart leaves my hand on the same arc as the last one and the one before it, and I am reaching for the next before it lands. The board has narrowed to one wedge. Somebody racks the pool balls behind me and I do not turn.
The gouge rides the tool rest and the bowl's inside opens up in one continuous ribbon that curls over my knuckles. I shift my feet and the cut keeps going. Shavings are up past my ankles.

The image comes up in the developer tray and I rock it under the red light, counting without numbers, lifting it at the moment the shadows arrive. Stop bath, fixer, the next sheet. I have been in here long enough that the rest of the house has gone to bed.

The spreadsheet's errors fall to a formula I write once and drag down the column, and the next error class is already visible in the sorted view. My coffee is cold and I am typing with both hands and reading with the rest of me. The cleaned file is nearly cleaned.

The compass needle and the contour lines and the slope under my boots agree, and I am running between the controls with the map folded in my thumb. The next flag is behind that knoll. My legs take the fall line without asking.

The bowline, the clove hitch, the cleat wrap, each line coming to hand in the order the boat needs them as we come alongside. The fenders squeak against the dock. My hands are done before the skipper finishes calling the sequence.
The plane takes a shaving the full length of the door edge in one pass and the next pass comes thinner. I sight down the edge and go again. The afternoon has become the sound of the blade.

The arrow is drawn and anchored and gone in a single motion I have stopped dividing into steps. The target is the only thing with edges. I nock the next one and the line of people behind me has gone silent or gone home.

The nib glides and the letters come out even and slanted the way the copybook shows, line after line down the page. My wrist floats above the paper. I turn the page and realize the ink bottle is half empty.

Three balls become a pattern and the pattern holds, my hands catching and throwing at a height my eyes have stopped checking. The kitchen ceiling is close and I do not hit it. Fifty catches, a hundred, and I lose count on purpose.

The stems go into the vase one at a time and each one tells me where the next one belongs. I turn the arrangement and cut another an inch shorter. The counter is covered in leaves and the shop door chimes for a customer I let my colleague take.

The code review is forty files deep and I am reading the diff the way I read a story, each change explaining the one before it. My comments go in short and exact. The standup I was supposed to attend ended an hour ago.

The lesson plan writes itself once the first activity clicks, each step handing off to the next, and I am filling in the margins with questions the kids will ask. The pen is running out and I switch without looking. The staff room has emptied around me.

The ice gives under the pick and holds under the crampon and I am moving up the frozen falls in a sequence of swings and kicks my body is choosing. The rope runs out below me. There is the next placement and nothing else.

The melody line wants a harmony a third below and my left hand finds it on the fretboard before I have named the note. The phone is recording and I have forgotten it. The song is writing the next bar for me.

The stone wall goes up one rock at a time, each one turned until it finds the face that sits, and the next one already in my eye before this one is down. My gloves are worn through at the fingertips. The row is level and the sun is lower than it was.

The text comes in at 1:40 in the morning and it just says home, two letters and a period. I put the phone face down on the nightstand and the breath I have been holding since midnight goes out of me all at once. My shoulders come down from somewhere near my ears.

The engine turns over on the third try and catches, and the dashboard lights settle into their normal pattern. I sit with my hands on the wheel and let it idle in the parking garage. The tow truck number is still on the screen of my phone and I do not need it.

The vet comes back with the x-ray and says the word clean before she says anything else. I hear the rest of it from a distance while the dog leans against my shin. In the parking lot I sit in the car for five minutes before I can drive.

The wallet is in the pocket of the coat I wore Tuesday, every card still in its slot. I stand in the closet holding it with my eyes shut. The list of numbers to call goes into the recycling folded in half.

The results page loads and my name is on the list of people who passed. I read it three times to make sure the alphabet has not fooled me. Then I laugh out loud in the empty kitchen and have to sit down on the floor.

The radar shows the red cell sliding north of us and the sirens stop one by one across town. I come up out of the basement with the flashlight still on. The windows are all where they were and the rain is only rain.

The surgeon pulls off her cap in the waiting room doorway and nods before she reaches us. Everything went the way it should, she says, and my mother's hand lets go of mine for the first time in four hours. I find I have been standing without knowing when I stood.

The email with the list goes around at ten and my name is not on it. I read the whole thing twice, then close the laptop and put both palms flat on the desk. The coffee I made at eight is still full and I drink it cold.

The furnace catches with a soft thump and the vents begin to breathe warm air into the hall. I stand over the register in my socks with my hands out. The space heater goes back in the closet with its cord wrapped.

The search team's radio crackles and the voice says they have him, cold and talking, a mile down the east fork. My legs give a little and I lean on the truck. Someone puts a blanket on my shoulders and I had not noticed I was shaking.

The agent types for a long minute and then says she has me on the six o'clock, window seat, no charge. I thank her more times than makes sense. The boarding pass prints and I hold it with both hands walking back to the gate.

The thermometer reads normal for the first time in three days and she is asking for toast. I sit on the edge of the bed and push the hair off her forehead. The bottle of medicine goes on the high shelf where it can stay.

The smoke alarm screams and I come running, and it is the bagel, blackened in the toaster and smoking like a tire. I wave a towel under the detector until it quits. My heart takes another minute to get the message.

The doctor says cyst and benign in the same sentence and keeps talking about follow-up in a year. I nod along and realize I have been gripping the edge of the paper-covered table. On the way out I hold the elevator for a stranger and smile at him like we are old friends.

The clerk slides the form back across the counter and says I am all set, the case is closed. I pick it up and the paper trembles a little in my hand. Outside the courthouse the sun is ordinary and I stand in it.

The mechanic wipes his hands and says it passed, nothing needed but the one bulb. I pay for the bulb and walk back to the car slower than I walked in. The sticker on the windshield is a different color now.

The back end slides on the ice and I steer into it and the tires catch, and the bridge is behind me and I am still in my lane. I pull into the gas station on the far side and turn the engine off. My hands are not steady enough for the gas cap yet.

The signature line is filled in and the contract is on its way back in the envelope they provided. I close the mailbox and stand on the sidewalk with my hand still on the handle. Six months of back and forth are in that slot.

The banking app refreshes and the rent payment shows as cleared, the balance sitting in the black with eleven dollars to spare. I set the phone on the table and lean back until the chair creaks. The first of the month is behind me.
The nurse says the rash is heat, nothing more, and shows me the cream in the drawer. My son is already bored and swinging his legs off the table. I hold him a bit too long putting his shirt back on.

Morning comes and the roof is still a roof, the gutters full of leaves but hanging where they belong. I walk the perimeter of the house in my boots and find one shingle in the yard. One shingle I can live with.
The refrigerator shudders back to life and the clock on the stove blinks twelve. I open the freezer and the ice cream is soft but still ice cream. The candles can burn themselves out on the counter.
The dentist leans back and says no cavities, see you in six months. I close my mouth and swallow and feel my whole jaw unlock. The receptionist asks if I want a sticker and I say yes.

The branch came down on the shed, not the house, and the shed was already leaning. I pick my way across the wet yard and look at the splintered roof and the intact kitchen window beside it. The chainsaw can wait until after coffee.

The interview ends with a handshake and the door closing behind me, and I walk to the elevator with my blazer already unbuttoned. In the lobby I stop and lean against the marble wall for a second. Whatever happens now, that part is done.
The refund posts four days later than they promised, the whole amount, and the hold on my card lifts. I buy groceries with it the same afternoon. The receipt goes in my pocket and stays there.

The phone sits in the rice for two days and then, when I hold the button, the logo comes up and the lock screen after it. Every photo is still there. I put it down on the dry towel and do not touch it again for an hour.
The earring is in the drain trap, caught in the hair and grime, both the post and the back. I rinse it under the tap and close my fist around it. My grandmother's face is suddenly very close.

The landlord says the building is not selling after all and the lease can run as written. I hang up and look around the apartment as if it had almost gone somewhere. The boxes I had flattened can go back under the bed.

The bus rounds the corner four minutes after the last one I thought I could catch, and the driver waits while I run the half block. I drop into a seat and let my bag slide to the floor. The interview is in forty minutes and the building is six stops away.

The loan officer calls to say approved before I have finished my sandwich. I say thank you and set the phone down and finish the sandwich very slowly. The folder of pay stubs on the table can go back in the drawer.

The last slide goes up and the questions are kind ones and then there is applause and I am sitting down. My knees take a moment to belong to me again. Someone hands me a glass of water and I drink all of it.

The teacher's voicemail turns out to be about the science fair, not the thing I was bracing for, and she sounds proud of him. I listen to it twice because the first time I did not hear the words. The kitchen chair takes my weight.
The recall notice lists model years that stop one year before ours. I check the sticker inside the driver's door twice to be certain. Then I put the kids' car seats back in the way they were.

The officer stamps the page, slides the passport back, and says welcome home. My bag comes around the carousel first, which has never happened. I walk out through the sliding doors into air that smells like diesel and rain.

Both feet are on the ground and the extension ladder is still leaning where I left it, and the gutter is clear. I sit on the back step with my hands between my knees. The ground feels very solid and I am in no hurry to leave it.

The bear looks at us for a long moment and then turns and ambles back into the trees without hurrying. We stand on the trail until the crashing stops. My wife laughs first and then I do, too loud, with the bear spray still in my hand.

The fire alarm turns out to be the drill the building emailed about last week and nobody read. We stand in the parking lot in the sun and then file back in. At my desk I sit for a minute before I touch the keyboard.
The passport is in the side pocket of the suitcase, where I would never put it, where I put it. The cab is still waiting at the curb with the meter running. I do not care about the meter.

The brake pads come out worn to the metal and the mechanic shows me how close it was. The new ones go on while I wait. Driving home I test them at the first stop sign and they take hold like a hand on my shoulder.

Her head comes up out of the lake, hair plastered flat, coughing and already yelling that she is fine. I am waist deep before I know I have walked in. She lets me carry her to the shore and then squirms down to go back.
The merge finishes with no conflicts and the test suite goes green on the first run. I lean back and the chair rolls a foot from the desk. Three days of untangling branches and it just goes.

The grades post and the number next to the class I was sure I had failed is a letter I can live with. I close the laptop and open it again to be sure it is still there. Then I call my mother to tell her nothing is wrong.

The plane's wheels touch and the cabin settles and the man next to me unclenches his hands from the armrest. I unclench mine. Through the window the terminal rolls toward us with its ordinary lights on.
The bleeding stops with the third towel and the cut, once I can see it, is long but shallow. I tape it closed and rinse the sink. My daughter is already asking whether she can go back outside.

The lab calls back and says the second test agrees with the first, and it is the one we wanted. I sit on the stairs halfway between the floors. The banister is cool under my hand and I hold it anyway.

The water comes back on with a cough and a spit and then runs clear from the kitchen tap. I fill the kettle and then a pot and then another pot for no reason. The plumber's estimate on the counter can go in the drawer with the others.

The dog trots up the driveway at dusk with his collar still on and a burr in his tail, as if he had been gone five minutes. I crouch down and he walks into my arms and I hold the back of his neck. The flyers are still in the printer tray.

The check clears and the number in the account goes from red to black for the first time this month. I take the phone off the charger and look at it again in the other room. Dinner can be something other than rice.

The principal says he was defending the smaller kid, not starting it, and the other parents agree. I let out a breath that moves the papers on her desk. Outside the office he is waiting on the bench with his backpack in his lap.

The inspector signs the form and says the wiring is up to code after all, the old report was wrong. I walk him to his truck and stand in the driveway after he leaves. The closing can happen Friday and I can sleep tonight.

The power steering groan turns out to be low fluid and nothing else, two dollars at the counter and a funnel. I top it off in the parking lot and turn the wheel lock to lock in silence. The quote from the other shop goes into the glovebox and out of my mind.

The ultrasound tech turns the screen and says there is the heartbeat, strong and fast, and points to the flicker. My husband's grip on my hand loosens by degrees. I had not noticed how cold the room was until I feel warm.

The train stops short of the station with a jolt and then creeps forward and the doors open where they should. The conductor says a signal fault, nothing more. I step onto the platform and my bag feels lighter than it did.

The missing file is in the trash folder, dated yesterday, all four hundred pages of it. I drag it back to the desktop and it opens. I save three copies in three places and then go outside and stand on the porch.

The toddler's choking cough turns into a wail, loud and indignant and full of air, and the piece of apple is on the floor. I hold her against my chest while she screams into my shirt. Screaming has never sounded so much like music.

The lake has not moved since I sat down and the only sound is the paddle dripping into the hull. Mist stands in the cove and the far shore is a gray line. I let the canoe drift and keep my hands in my lap.
I am the first one up and the kitchen is blue with early light. The kettle has not boiled yet and I am in no hurry for it to. Out the window the frost is leaving the lawn one blade at a time.

The inbox has sixty messages and I open them one at a time, read each to the end, and answer or file it before touching the next. My breath is even and my shoulders are where they belong. The clock on the wall is doing its job and I am doing mine.

Snow is falling on the empty road and I am walking in the middle of it because there is no one else. Each step squeaks and then there is nothing. My hands are deep in my pockets and my breath hangs and goes.

The monks finish the chant and the hall goes silent except for the pigeons in the rafters. I sit on the cool stone with my legs folded under me and my palms open on my knees. A stick of incense burns down and I watch the ash hold its shape.
The highway is empty at this hour and the dashed lines come toward me at a speed I could keep up forever. The radio is off. The hills on either side go from black to gray to the first green.

My grandfather does not say much anymore, so we sit by his window and watch the birds at the feeder. His hand is on the armrest and mine is on the back of his chair. A cardinal lands and he lifts one finger to point it out.
The tide is going out and leaving the sand smooth and dark behind it. I walk the line where the wet meets the dry with my shoes in one hand. Each wave reaches a little less far than the one before.
The baby has fallen asleep on my chest and her breath is a warm patch through my shirt. I match my breathing to hers without meaning to. The dishwasher finishes its cycle and I do not get up.

The garden hose makes a sound against the leaves like rain that has decided to be gentle. I move down the row one plant at a time, counting nothing. The light is going gold at the edges of everything.
The train has emptied out by the fourth stop and I have the whole car and the long light across the seats. Fields pass and I let them. My bag is on the floor and my hands are folded on my knee.

The rain started an hour ago and shows no sign of stopping, which suits the afternoon. I lie on the couch with my feet on the armrest and listen to it work on the roof. The book has closed on my chest and I have let it.
The neighbor stops on the front path to talk about his tomatoes and I lean on the rake and let him. The sun is on the side of my face. Neither of us checks the time.
Bread dough is rising under a towel on the counter and the house smells of yeast and the window is open. I wipe the flour off the board in slow circles. There is nothing to do for an hour but wait.

The last patient has left and I sit in the exam room with the lights dimmed and my hands loose on the desk. The chart is finished. Through the wall I can hear the receptionist humming while she locks up.

The mountain pass opens up and I pull onto the gravel shoulder and turn off the engine. The valley below is in shadow and the peaks across it are in sun. I stand with my hand on the warm hood and breathe the thin air.
The cat kneads the blanket on my lap and settles, and her purr goes up through my thigh. I rest my hand along her back and feel it rise and fall. The lamp is the only light on in the house.
The sauna door closes and the heat wraps around me and the cedar ticks. Water hisses on the stones and the steam rolls up to the ceiling. I lean my head back against the wall and let my arms hang.

The rowing shell cuts the river at dawn and the oars drip in unison on the recovery. The coxswain has stopped calling and I am rowing to the sound of the water with the seven others. The bridge passes over us and its shadow is cool.
I pour the tea from a height so it cools on the way down and the steam rises in a thin thread. The cup warms both my hands. Outside the window the bamboo moves and comes back.
The hammock swings a little in a wind I can barely feel and the leaves go on with their business overhead. My eyes are half closed. A plane passes very high and leaves a line that slowly widens.
The church is empty on a Tuesday and the light comes through the colored glass in slabs across the pews. I sit near the back with my coat still on. The radiators knock and settle and knock again.
The dog and I have walked this field every morning for nine years and the path knows our feet. Dew soaks the cuffs of my jeans. She ranges ahead and comes back and ranges ahead again.

The fishing line hangs slack in water the color of tea and the bobber has not moved in an hour. I am leaning against a tree root that fits my back exactly. A heron stands on one leg across the pond and we ignore each other.

The pool is empty at six in the morning and I swim slow lengths with my face in the water and the black line beneath me. Breathe, three strokes, breathe. The wall comes and I turn and the wall comes again.
The old woman at the next table feeds crumbs to the sparrows and the waiter lets her. My espresso has a thin crema and the square is in shade. I have nowhere to be until the museum opens at ten.

The horse's breath steams in the barn aisle and I brush the dust off her flank in long strokes. She shifts her weight and sighs through her nose. The morning light comes in sideways through the gaps in the boards.
The waiting room has one other person in it and a fish tank, and I watch the angelfish turn in the light. My name will be called when it is called. I cross my ankles and let my hands rest on my coat.

The vines run in rows down the hill to the river and I walk between them with my hand brushing the leaves. The grapes are weeks from ready. Somewhere below a tractor is working and the sound comes and goes with the wind.

The candle has burned down an inch and the dinner plates are pushed back and no one has moved to clear them. My wife's hand rests on the table near mine. The conversation has thinned to a few words at a time and that is enough.

The ferry pulls away from the dock and the island gets smaller behind us in the gray light. I stand at the stern rail with the wind coming straight through my jacket. Gulls follow us for a while and then turn back.
The library reading room is nearly empty and the green lamps are on along the long tables. I have one book open and another waiting. Someone turns a page across the room and the sound carries.

The desert road runs straight to the horizon and the sky is bigger than any sky I have been under. I drive with one hand and the window down. The radio lost its station an hour ago and I never looked for another.
Snow has filled the back yard overnight and no one has walked in it, not even the dog. I stand on the step in my boots and do not go out yet. The pine branches bow under their load and hold.

The loom is quiet for the day and the half-finished cloth hangs with the light behind it, every thread where it should be. I run my palm across the woven part. The shuttle rests on the bench where I set it down.
The old dog sleeps in the sun on the porch and his paws twitch after something. I sit beside him on the boards and lean against the post. The street is empty and the mail will come when it comes.
The last page of the ledger balances and I set the pen down parallel to the edge of the desk. Rain is beginning in the courtyard. I fold my hands and watch it darken the stones one at a time.

The meadow is loud with insects and nothing else, and I am lying with the grass over my face and the sky in pieces between the stems. My heartbeat slows to match something out here. A hawk passes over and does not stop.
The brush dips and the water on the paper takes the pigment where it wants to go. I am not steering it much. The wash dries at its own speed and I sit back and let it.
The nursing baby has let go and is asleep with her mouth open and my shirt still pushed up. The room is dark except for the hall light. I could put her down and I do not.
The city is below the roof and its noise reaches me as one even hum. I lean on the parapet with a mug cooling in my hands. The sun is coming up behind the water towers and taking its time.

The orchard is bare and the ladders are put away and the ground is soft with fallen leaves. I walk the rows with my hands behind my back the way my father did. The trees have done their work for the year and so have I.
The bath has gone from hot to warm and I have not moved. The faucet drips at a pace I could set a watch by. Steam has fogged the mirror and I cannot see myself and do not need to.
The chess game has reached an ending where nothing can be forced and we both know it. My grandfather moves his king one square and I move mine. The clock between us has stopped mattering.
The kayak noses into the reeds and I ship the paddle and let the current turn me. Dragonflies work the surface. The sun is on my forearms and the water smells of mud and summer.
The hospital chapel has no one in it and the lights are low and the chairs are soft. I sit with my elbows on my knees and my eyes on the carpet. For ten minutes nobody needs anything from me.

The night shift is over and I am sitting in the car in the lot watching the sky go pale behind the building. The engine is off and the keys are in my lap. Birds are starting in the hedge by the entrance.
The blanket is tucked around my knees and the porch swing moves an inch each way without my pushing it. Fog sits in the low field. Somewhere a cow is complaining and nothing else is.
The last guest has gone to bed and I sit in the kitchen with the lights off and the moon on the floor. The refrigerator hums. I can hear the house breathing around me and I am breathing with it.
The yoga teacher stops talking and the room is just the sound of twenty people breathing on their backs. My palms are up and heavy. The ceiling fan turns slowly and I watch one blade go around.
The vineyard dog walks with me to the end of the row and sits when I sit. The valley is filling with evening and the lights of the town are coming on far below. We watch them until they are all on.

The old man beside me on the bench has fallen asleep in the sun and his hat has slipped forward. The pigeons work the gravel around our feet. I keep my hands in my lap and let the afternoon pass over both of us.

The piano is open and I play the same slow piece I have played for thirty years, the one my hands know better than my name. The window is open and the curtain lifts and drops. The last chord hangs and I let it fade on its own.

The sheep have moved to the far side of the hill and the field between us is empty and green. I sit on the stone wall with my boots dangling. A cloud shadow crosses the grass and takes its time about it.
My daughter sleeps in the next seat with her head on my arm and the plane hums over an ocean I cannot see. The cabin lights are off. I have a book open and have not turned the page in a long while.
The last of the dishes are done and the towel is hung on the oven door and the kitchen is exactly as it should be. I lean against the counter and look at it. The clock ticks and I let it tick.

Three missed calls from the school and a voicemail that cuts off after the word incident. I am dialing back with one hand and grabbing my keys with the other and the line is busy. My throat has closed to the width of a straw.

Water is coming through the ceiling light fixture in a steady stream and the bowl I put under it is already full. I am on the phone with the landlord's voicemail and shouting at it. The carpet squelches under my feet and the stain is spreading toward the outlet.

She was in the cereal aisle and now she is not, and the cart is where I left it and the store is enormous. I say her name louder each time and people are starting to look. My hands have gone cold and my voice has climbed somewhere I do not recognize.

There is smoke coming under the apartment door and the alarm in the hall has started, and the cat is somewhere under the bed. I am on my knees sweeping my arm into the dark and calling her. My eyes are streaming and I cannot tell if it is the smoke.

The dog is in my arms and the car that hit him is gone and his breathing is wrong, fast and shallow and with a sound in it. I am running toward the house and shouting for someone to get the keys. His blood is warm through my shirt.

The doors to the back say staff only and my father went through them on a gurney forty minutes ago and no one has come out. I have asked the desk twice. I am standing because sitting feels like giving something up.

The account page loads and the balance is wrong, and then I scroll and the charges keep coming, one after another, cities I have never been to. The hold music has been playing for eleven minutes. I am pacing the kitchen with the phone pressed hard enough to hurt.

The brake pedal goes soft halfway down the hill and the car keeps gaining and the intersection at the bottom has a light I cannot see yet. I am pumping the pedal and grabbing for the handbrake and the kids are asking what is wrong. My whole body has become the pedal.

His lips are swelling and he is pulling at his collar and the hives are coming up on his neck while I watch. I am tearing the cap off the pen with my teeth. My hands are shaking so much I have to steady one with the other.

The phone died an hour ago and the streets have stopped matching anything I remember and no one I stop speaks a language I have. It is past midnight and the shops are shuttered. I keep walking because standing still feels worse.

The notice is taped to the door at eye level with a date fourteen days out. I read it standing in the hallway with the groceries going soft at my feet. The baby is crying inside and I cannot make my hand turn the key.

My sister's voice says Mom fell and then something about the stairs and an ambulance and I have stopped hearing the words. I am already pulling a bag out of the closet with nothing in it. The phone slides off my shoulder and I grab for it twice.
The crowd surges forward and my feet leave the ground for a second and the air goes out of my chest against the back of a stranger. I cannot get my arms up. Someone is screaming and it might be me.

The water in the bottom of the boat is over my ankles now and the bilge pump is making a sound instead of pumping. I am bailing with a cooler lid and losing. The shore is a long gray line that is not getting closer.

The laptop screen goes black in front of two hundred people and the clicker in my hand does nothing. I am pressing the power button and talking and neither is working. Sweat runs down my back under the jacket and the silence in the room has a weight to it.

The passport is not in the bag and the bag is on the floor with everything in it spread across the terminal carpet. They are calling final boarding for my row. I am going through the same three pockets again and again as if they will change.

The thermometer says a number I have only read about and the car will not turn over and it is three in the morning. She is limp against my shoulder and too hot to hold comfortably. I am dialing with a thumb that keeps missing.

The file opens to garbage, rows of symbols where the report was, and the deadline is in two hours and the backup is from last week. I am clicking recover and undo and recover again. My stomach has dropped through the floor and stayed there.
The message from my friend reads like a goodbye and she is not answering her phone and it goes to voicemail each time. I am in the car with no shoes on. The red lights take years.

The windows are bowing in and out with the gusts and the kids are in the bathtub with the mattress over them like I read to do. The roof makes a sound I have never heard a roof make. I am crouched beside them with my hand on the mattress and I cannot stop talking.

The oil flares up the side of the pan and the flame reaches the cabinet before I understand what I am seeing. I grab the lid and miss and grab it again. The smoke is black and the alarm is going and my son is in the doorway.

The wrapper on the floor is from the dark chocolate bar and the dog is panting and it was most of the bar. The emergency vet is forty minutes away and not answering. I am in the car with him in my lap and the wrapper in my pocket and my foot too hard on the gas.

The pressure comes across my chest at the top of the stairs at the gym and my left arm goes strange. I sit down on the step and the room swims a little. Someone is asking if I am all right and I cannot get enough air to answer.

The doctor is saying words with too many syllables and the word serious and asking if I have someone who can drive me. I am nodding at the carpet. My hands are gripping the chair arms and I cannot feel them.

The text from the school says lockdown and then says do not come to the campus and then says nothing else for nineteen minutes. I am standing in the driveway with my keys in my hand. Every car on the street sounds like a siren.

The water in the basement is at the second step and rising and the furnace is in it and so is the box with the photographs. I am carrying things up the stairs two at a time and setting them down anywhere. My jeans are soaked to the thigh and I have stopped noticing the cold.

The security guard is walking me to the door with a box in my arms and my badge already gone and people are not looking up from their desks. The elevator takes a long time to come. My face is hot and I cannot make it stop.

The airbag dust is still in the air and the horn is stuck on and I cannot find the latch for the seatbelt. The other car is sideways across the lane. I am saying are you okay to the passenger seat where no one is sitting.

The elevator stopped between floors twenty minutes ago and the alarm button makes a sound no one answers and the phone has no signal. The walls are closer than they were. I am breathing through my mouth and counting the ceiling tiles again.

The letter from the lawyer uses the word custody four times on the first page. I read it standing at the mailbox and then again in the kitchen and the words do not rearrange themselves. The pot on the stove is boiling over and I am watching it do it.

The kitten's sides are going in and out too fast and her mouth is open and she will not lift her head. I am wrapping her in a dish towel and dropping my keys. The clinic closes in ten minutes and it is fifteen away.

The oven died an hour ago and the first guests are on the porch and the cake is raw in the middle and the dog has eaten the cheese off the board. I am smiling at the door with flour on my face. Behind me something is beeping and I do not know what.

The exam booklet is open and the first question is in a language I studied for a year and cannot read right now. The clock has eaten twelve minutes. My pen is pressing hard enough to dent the page and nothing is on it.

The bag is lighter and the zipper is open and the wallet and passport and phone are gone, and the train is pulling out of a station whose name I cannot pronounce. I pat the same pockets again. My face is wet and I have not decided to cry.

Dad's chair is empty and the front door is open and his shoes are still by the mat. It is dark and he does not know the street anymore. I am running down the block in my socks calling him by his first name.

The all-hands email says the names will go out at two and it is one fifty and the office has gone silent in a way that has texture. I am staring at the clock in the corner of the screen. My coffee has gone cold in my hand and I have not put it down.

It is two in the morning and he said midnight and his phone goes straight to voicemail and his location has stopped sharing. I have called his friends and woken two of their parents. I am standing at the front window with my coat on over my pajamas.

The gas smell is strongest in the kitchen and getting stronger and I cannot remember if you are supposed to open the windows or not touch anything. I am herding the kids toward the front door. My hands will not work the deadbolt on the first try.

My hiking partner is at the bottom of the scree with her leg bent in a direction legs do not go, and she is not making a sound, which is worse. I am sliding down toward her and the rocks are moving under me. There is no signal up here and I knew that this morning.

The bill has a number on it with a comma in a place I was not ready for and the words patient responsibility. I read it at the kitchen counter with my coat still on. The number does not get smaller the more I look.
The hard drive clicks three times and goes quiet and the folder with four years of thesis does not appear. I unplug it and plug it back in and it clicks again. I am saying no out loud to the desk.

The shouting through the wall has stopped being words and there was a crash and now there is nothing. I am standing in my hallway with my phone in my hand and my thumb over the numbers. The silence next door is louder than the shouting was.

The officer's hand is on his belt and my son is crying in the back seat and I am trying to reach the registration without moving too fast. My voice comes out thin and too polite. The flashlight is in my eyes and I cannot see his face.

The connecting gate closed four minutes ago and the board says the next flight is tomorrow and the agent is shaking her head before I finish the sentence. My carry-on strap has cut a line into my shoulder. I am asking the same question a third way.

The mare is down in the stall and rolling and her sides are heaving and it is midnight and the vet's line is ringing and ringing. I am in the stall with her trying to get her up. Her breath is hot on my hands and she is groaning.

The pot handle is turning as the toddler reaches for it and I am across the kitchen and the water is boiling and everything slows down and speeds up at once. I am lunging with my arm out. My shout comes out before I decide to make it.

The man at the next table has stopped talking and his face is going dark and his wife is slapping his back and nothing is coming out. I am up out of my chair with my napkin still in my hand. Someone is yelling for a doctor and the room has gone very loud.

The pension letter says the fund is being restructured and uses the word reduced in a sentence I have read six times. My wife is asking what it means from the other room. I do not have an answer and my hands are not steady enough to fold it back up.

My mother-in-law slides sideways out of her chair in the middle of grace and her plate goes with her. Everyone is up and nobody is doing anything useful and I am one of them. Someone has to call and I am looking at my own phone as if it belongs to someone else.

The floor is moving and the glasses are walking off the shelf one at a time and the sound is coming from everywhere. I am under the table with my arms over my daughter's head. It is not stopping and it is not stopping.

The two dogs have each other by the neck and the sound they are making is not a sound I knew dogs could make. I am pulling on a collar and getting nowhere and someone is screaming to grab the back legs. There is blood on the grass and I cannot tell whose.

The door has locked behind me and the baby is inside on the changing table and my keys and phone are on the counter. I can hear her starting to cry through the window. I am pounding on the neighbor's door with the flat of my hand.

The monitor by his bed starts an alarm I have not heard before and two nurses come in fast and one of them asks me to step out. I step out and stand against the wall of the corridor. My back is pressed to the paint and my hands are flat against it.

The lawyer repeats the question slower and my own words from an email three years ago are on the screen in front of me. The court reporter's hands have stopped. I can feel my pulse in my neck and I am sure everyone can see it.

The ice makes a sound like a rifle and a line opens between my skates and the far bank. I am going flat and spreading my weight and the water is right there under the crack. My daughter is behind me on the shore and I am telling her to stay there in a voice I do not recognize.

The sirens start while the kids are in the deep end and the lifeguard is blowing a whistle no one is obeying. The sky to the west has gone a green I have only seen in photographs. I am at the edge of the pool shouting their names and they cannot hear me over the horn.

The login page sends the verification code to a phone number I have not had in four years, and the link to change the number is behind the login. I type my password a fifth time as if that will help. My jaw has set itself and my finger is hitting the keys harder than keys need.

The jar lid will not turn under the towel or the rubber grip or the hot water, and the recipe is waiting with the onions already going brown. I rap the edge on the counter twice and try again and my palm slips. The pickles are an inch away behind glass.

The printer says paper jam and there is no paper jammed anywhere I can open, and the meeting is in six minutes. I pull out the tray and slide it back in and the message does not change. My breath is coming out through my nose in short hard bursts.

The fourth transfer drops me back into the same hold music I started in forty minutes ago, with the same recording about unusually high call volume. I have explained the problem three times to three people. The phone is hot against my ear and I am gripping it like it might get away.

Step eleven calls for a screw the bag does not contain, and the holes in panel C do not line up with the holes in panel D by about a quarter inch. I have taken the back off twice. The instruction sheet has a drawing of a smiling man and I would like a word with him.

The phone changes her name to a word every single time and I go back and fix it every single time and send it anyway and it has changed again. I type it letter by letter with a pause between each. The autocorrect suggestion bar sits there smug and blue.

The parking meter rejects the card, then rejects the other card, then rejects the coins I dig out of the console because one of them is Canadian. The appointment is across the street and started two minutes ago. I slap the side of the machine with my palm and it does nothing.

The self-checkout says unexpected item in the bagging area for the third time and there is nothing in the bagging area but the bag. The light on the pole is blinking for an attendant who is helping someone else. I lift the bag and set it down and the machine thinks about it.

The wet knot in my son's shoelace has pulled into a hard little bead and my nails cannot get a purchase on it. The bus is at the corner. I pick and pick and the lace only tightens and he is hopping on one foot telling me to hurry.

The worksheet wants the subtraction done a way I have never seen, with boxes and arrows, and my way gets the right answer and a red mark. My daughter is crying because I am doing it wrong. I am pressing the pencil hard enough to snap the lead and I have snapped it.

The merge lane has been closed for a mile with cones and every car that passes on the shoulder is going to cut in at the front. I keep two lengths back and three more cars slide into the gap. My knuckles are white on the wheel and I am talking to the windshield.

The update started itself at eight fifty and the bar says twelve percent and the slides for nine are on this machine. I click the cancel button that does not cancel. Every muscle in my neck has pulled tight and I am staring at a spinning circle.

The zipper on the coat has caught the lining and will go neither up nor down, and I am already late and it is cold enough that going without is not an option. I pull it and the fabric bunches tighter. I say a word out loud in the empty hallway.

The television has three remotes and the one that changes the input has batteries that are dead, and the one that is not dead changes everything except the input. I am pressing buttons in combinations. The game started six minutes ago and I can hear the crowd through a blue screen.

The clerk slides the form back and says it is the old version and points to a stack of new ones, which look identical, and the line behind me is out the door. I fill out the new one at the counter with a pen on a chain. The number I pull from the dispenser is forty-one places back.

The mower cord comes out and goes back and the engine coughs and does not catch, eight times, nine, with the grass up to my shins and rain coming tonight. I check the choke again. My shoulder burns and I pull once more out of spite.

The video call freezes on my own face mid-sentence and comes back with everyone looking at me and someone saying you cut out. I say the sentence again and freeze again. I am leaning toward the router as if nearness were a signal.

The bank rejects the form because my signature does not match the one on file from when I was twenty-two. I sign it again, slower, trying to remember how I used to make the capital. The teller holds the two side by side and shakes her head.
The cumin has been moved from the aisle where it has been for nine years and no one in a vest knows where it went. I have walked the store twice. My cart has one thing in it and my list has twelve.

The thread goes to the eye of the needle and bends away, again, again, and I lick it and twist it and it splays. The lamp is right on it and my eyes are watering. The hem has been waiting since last winter.

The phone system says I did not catch that and offers the same five options, none of which is the thing I need. I say representative in every tone I own. My free hand is drumming the counter hard enough to rattle the fruit bowl.

I have asked my brother whether he is coming Thursday four times by text and twice on the phone and each answer is a question back. The caterer needs a number by five. I type the question a fifth time and delete the sentence I added after it.

The contractor's truck is not in the driveway at eight, or at nine, and his phone goes to a voicemail box that is full. This is the third morning I have stayed home. The hole in the wall looks exactly the way it looked in March.

Nine hundred and ninety-nine pieces are in place and the thousandth is not in the box, not under the table, not in the dog's bed. I have looked in the vacuum bag. The sky has a hole in it the shape of a question.

The cat has been sick on the one rug in the house that cannot go in the machine, and not on the tile a foot away. I am on my knees with the spray and the paper towels. She watches me from the chair with her tail going.

The cable I need is in the tangle behind the desk and every cable I pull brings three others with it and one of them is the monitor. I have unplugged the lamp twice. My arm is wedged between the desk and the wall and my face is in the dust.

The tax website times out on the final submit page and sends me back to the beginning, with the fields empty, for the second time tonight. I type my address again with my teeth together. The deadline is midnight and the clock on the screen says eleven forty.

One bulb somewhere in the string of two hundred is out and so all two hundred are out, and I am going along the gutter in the cold pressing each one in turn. The ladder shifts a little every time I lean. The neighbors' lights have been up and lit for a week.

The cart's front wheel shudders and drags left and I correct it every three steps up and down every aisle. I switched carts once already and got this one. By the frozen section I am steering with both forearms and my teeth.

He will not put the shoes on, not the blue ones, not the other ones, and daycare closes its doors at nine and it is eight fifty. I kneel and he goes limp like a sack. My voice is getting louder and I can hear it and I cannot bring it down.

The snowblower chute packs solid every six feet of the driveway and I stop and clear it with the stick and go six more feet. The snow is the heavy wet kind. My gloves are soaked and I have been at this an hour and the mailbox is still a long way off.

We are on item four of nine on an agenda that could have been a paragraph, and item four is a question that was answered in item two. I click my pen and uncap it and cap it. The clock on the wall is behind me and I have turned around to check it three times.

The cell says REF and every cell that depends on it says REF and the column I need for the report is a column of REF. I undo back twenty steps and it is still there. I am squinting at a formula I wrote and cannot read.

The fitted sheet will not fold into anything but a ball, no matter which corner goes into which, and the video I watched made it look like origami. I shake it out and start over. My arms ache from holding it up and the ball is getting bigger.

The vending machine takes the dollar and the coil turns and the bag of pretzels hangs there by one corner, not falling. I press the button again and it wants another dollar. I lean my forehead against the glass and look at it hanging.

The second coat has dried and every pass of the roller shows as a stripe in the afternoon light, and the room looked perfect at noon. I take the roller back out of the bag. My wrist aches and the paint can has an inch left.

The sprinkler head will not turn to face the lawn and every time I bend to adjust it the next head in the line comes on and soaks my back. I have turned the water off twice to do this. My shirt is stuck to me and the driveway is wetter than the grass.

The screw head is stripped to a smooth dish and the driver spins in it with a sound that goes through my teeth. I try the rubber band trick and the pliers and the other pliers. The shelf hangs by one bracket at an angle that mocks me.

The childproof cap turns and turns and does not come off, and I am an adult with a headache standing in my own bathroom pressing down and twisting. The arrows on the cap do not line up with anything. I squeeze until my thumb goes white.

The map voice says turn left onto a street that is one way in the other direction and then recalculates into a loop that brings me back to the same intersection. This is the third time I have seen this bakery. I am saying no to the dashboard.

The maintenance request has been marked resolved for the second time and the radiator is still cold enough to keep milk on. I take a photo of the thermostat and attach it and type the same paragraph again. My fingers are stiff from the cold and the typos pile up.

The text says five minutes and the last text that said five minutes was twenty minutes ago and the host has given our table away once. I check the door and the phone and the door. The ice in my water has melted and I am crunching what is left.

The password reset email does not arrive, not in the inbox, not in spam, and the resend button says wait ten minutes. I have waited ten minutes three times. The show is paused on the title screen and my wife has gone to bed.

The recipe skips from the dough resting to the dough being rolled without saying how long, and the dough is a paste that sticks to everything. I add flour and it is a rock. The bowl goes into the sink harder than it needs to.

No to the toast, no to the eggs, no to the cereal she asked for, no to the banana she is holding. I am standing at the counter with four plates and a clock. My smile is a thing I am doing with my teeth.

The shower curtain wraps itself around my leg every time the water gets warm and I peel it off and it comes back. I have moved the liner inside and outside. I am standing in the corner of the tub with my elbow out like a fence.

The dog lunges toward every tree and every hydrant and every other dog and my shoulder is halfway out of its socket by the second block. I shorten the leash and he coughs and pulls anyway. We have gone two hundred yards in fifteen minutes.

The phone camera locks onto the head of the man in front of me and my daughter is a blur on the stage behind his ear. I tap the screen and it finds the curtain. Her solo is eight bars long and three of them are gone.

The committee has reopened the question we settled in March, with the same three objections from the same person, and the chair is letting it happen. I have the minutes from March in my bag. I am writing the word decided on my notepad and underlining it until the pen goes through.

The tiny screw from the glasses hinge is under the refrigerator somewhere and the flashlight shows dust and a penny and no screw. I have been on my stomach on the tile for ten minutes. The lens is on the counter looking at me.

The ski binding will not click with the glove on and will not click with the glove off because my fingers have gone numb, and the lift line is moving without me. Snow is packed into the sole. I stamp down for the sixth time and the binding spits the boot back out.

The tire bead will not seat on one side and the pump head keeps popping off the valve with a hiss that takes all the air I put in. I have levered the tire off and on twice. My thumbs are raw and the ride left ten minutes ago.

The crossword clue has a typo and the answer that fits the squares does not fit the clue and the answer that fits the clue has one letter too many. I have erased the corner three times and the paper is going thin. I put the pen down and pick it up again.

The hotel key card works on the third swipe, then not at all, then the front desk re-codes it and it works once and dies again by the time I reach the room with the luggage. The hallway is long and the ice bucket is heavy. I say the room number to the door as if it were listening.

The return label will not print because the browser wants a plugin and the plugin wants a restart and the post office closes at five. I take a screenshot and the screenshot will not attach. The box is taped and addressed and going nowhere.

The earbuds pair with my laptop when I want the phone and with the phone when I want the laptop and with the television once for reasons no one can explain. I hold the button until the light blinks and it connects to the wrong thing again. I take them out and put them in my pocket and listen to the bus.

The second shift ended twenty minutes ago and I am still sitting in the car in the lot with the keys in my hand. The steering wheel is cold and I have not turned the engine on. My eyes close on their own and I let them for a count of ten.

The baby went down at four and is up at five and I am standing at the crib with my eyes half shut, swaying from habit. My arms are lead from the shoulder down. The clock says a number I decide not to read.

Nine hours on the interstate and the last exit is still forty miles off and the coffee stopped working around hour six. I crack the window and the cold does nothing. My hands are at ten and two because I no longer trust them anywhere else.

I have turned him in the bed and changed the sheets and given the pills and it is only two in the afternoon. The chair by his bed has my shape in it now. I sit back down and the ceiling swims a little and I let it.

Forty essays are graded and twenty-two are not and the red pen has started to feel heavy. I read the same paragraph three times and it does not go in. The kitchen clock has stopped making sense and the tea is cold.

The truck is unloaded and the boxes are in rooms that are roughly right and the mattress is on the floor. I lie down on it in my shoes. Every joint has its own small complaint and I listen to none of them.
The last mile of the trail is all downhill and my knees have stopped cushioning anything. Each step lands and I feel it in my teeth. The parking lot is a rumor somewhere below the trees.

It is the third night in the chair beside the hospital bed and the chair has stopped pretending to be comfortable. The monitor beeps on a rhythm I know in my sleep now. I rest my forehead on the bed rail and the metal is cool.

The last table left at eleven and the floor is mopped and the chairs are up and my feet have gone past hurting into something flat. I count the drawer twice because the first count did not stick. The walk to the bus stop is four blocks and I think about each one.

The plane lands at six in the morning in a city where my body thinks it is midnight and the line for customs folds back on itself nine times. I shuffle forward with the bag strap cutting into my shoulder. My face feels like it belongs to someone who has been awake longer than me.
The last bin of apples is on the trailer and the light is going and my hands have stopped closing all the way. I lean on the tailgate. The rows I picked today look the same as the rows I have not.

Three exams in two days and the fourth is tomorrow and the textbook pages have begun to slide past without leaving anything behind. I am reading with my chin in my hand and my hand is losing. The library lights buzz and I could sleep under them.

The train home is standing room only and I am leaning against the pole with my eyes closed and my bag between my feet. Every stop the doors open and the cold comes in and I do not move. The week has had eleven days in it.

It is the ninth hour on the register two days before the holiday and the line has not been shorter than twelve since noon. I say the same four sentences and my mouth does them without me. My lower back has become a single dull note.

The dish pit is finally empty at one in the morning and my hands are white and wrinkled to the wrist. I peel off the gloves and they come away like a second skin. The bus does not run this late and the walk is uphill.

I have read the bedtime book twice and sung the song three times and he is still asking for water. My voice has gone flat and I can hear it. I sit on the floor by the bed because standing up again seems like a lot to ask.

Six hours in the waiting room and the number on the screen has moved eleven places. The chair has no back that my back recognizes. I have read every poster twice and the vending machine has nothing left I want.

The fifth interview of the day is at four and I am in the lobby in the same suit, smoothing the same folder. My face has smiled so much it feels borrowed. I say my name to the receptionist and it sounds like a word I am still learning.
