The kitchen has been a construction site for four months and tonight I am washing dishes in the bathtub again with sawdust in my hair. The microwave is on the floor of the living room. I dry a plate and sit down on the edge of the tub with it in my lap.

Mile twenty-two and my legs are running on something other than me and the crowd noise has gone far away. Each stride is a negotiation. I keep my eyes on the back of the runner ahead because looking further is more than I can do.

A week of two-hour nights and the words on the screen have started to drift when I stop looking directly at them. I type a sentence and read it back and it is not a sentence. My eyes are sand and the blinking does not help.
The calves are fed and the gate is fixed and the tractor is under the roof and it is dark and I am still in the yard. My boots weigh what they weigh. The porch light is a long way across the gravel.

Twelve hours on the ward and the handover is done and I am sitting in the break room with my shoes off and my feet on the opposite chair. The coffee pot has a quarter inch of something in it. I look at it and decide it is too far.

Six hundred miles today and the truck stop lights are too bright and the shower token is in my pocket and I cannot make myself walk to the building. I sit in the cab with the engine ticking. The next load picks up at five.

The twins are finally asleep at the same time for the first time today and I am lying on the floor between the cribs because that is where I was standing. The carpet is fine. The monitor light blinks green and I watch it blink.

Day three of the conference and the badge lanyard has worn a groove in my neck and the talks have merged into one long slide. I am in the back row with my coat on. Someone asks a question and I nod at it from very far away.

The last relative has driven off and the turkey carcass is in a bag and the table is a field of crumpled napkins. I sit at the end of it with my apron still on. The dishwasher is full and the sink is full and I will get to them.

The week of the funeral is over and the casseroles are stacked in the freezer and the thank-you cards are in a pile I cannot look at. I sit on the stairs with my coat half off. Every part of me is heavy in a way that sleep did not touch.

The release went out at four in the morning and the bugs came in at six and I am looking at a stack trace with my cheek on my fist. The keyboard has a wet spot where my coffee was. My thoughts arrive one at a time and slowly.

Seven meetings back to back and the last one ran long and my voice has gone to gravel. I close the laptop and the room is suddenly very quiet. My shoulders will not come down from where they have been all day.

The last box comes off the truck and my back makes a sound and I set it down wherever it lands. The stairs to the third floor are behind me forty times. I lean against the doorframe and the doorframe does most of the work.

The driveway is shoveled for the second time today, after work, in the dark, and the plow has already pushed a new wall across the end of it. I stand with the shovel upright like a flag. My arms hang and the snow keeps coming.

The third feed of the night and I am in the rocking chair with the bottle at an angle and my head against the wall. The night light makes the room orange. I count her swallows to stay awake and lose count.

Friday at three fifteen and the last class has gone and I am sitting at my desk with twenty-eight chairs in front of me, all empty, all crooked. The whiteboard still has the morning's problem on it. I do not have it in me to erase it yet.

The billable day ended at nine and I am still at the desk with the file open and the words not landing. The building is silent except for the vacuum somewhere below. I put my glasses on the desk and press my palms into my eyes.

Call number one hundred and six and the script is coming out of me without my hearing it anymore. The headset has worn the top of my ear raw. The clock on the wall is a thing I have stopped believing in.

The ferry is two hours late and the terminal benches are steel and the kids have run out of everything, including the will to complain. I am holding the sleeping one and the other is leaning on my knee. My arm went numb a while ago and I have left it that way.

The laundry is a mountain on the bed and the mountain has to be moved before anyone can sleep in the bed. I fold one shirt and sit down on the corner. The shirt is in my lap and the rest of the mountain is where it was.

It is eleven at night and raining and the dog has to go out and I am standing under the streetlight in a coat over pajamas holding the leash. He takes his time. I lean on the lamppost and the lamppost holds.

The last guest is gone and the tent is still up and the rented glasses are in crates and I am sitting in a folding chair in the middle of the lawn. My shoes are off beside me and the dew is coming up. The lights are still on in the trees and I do not have the arms to take them down.
Fourteen hours on and the bus home is warm and I am fighting to keep my head from going against the window. It goes against the window. The stop announcements come from somewhere underwater.

The defense is over and the committee has shaken my hand and I am in the hallway with my laptop bag and nowhere to put myself. Five years landed in two hours. I sit on the floor against the lockers because the floor is there.

The warehouse shift ends at six in the morning and the sky outside the dock door is going gray and my scanner hand has a claw shape it will not let go of. I punch out and stand by the time clock. The parking lot is a long bright rectangle.

The flight is canceled and the next one is at seven and the airport chairs have armrests designed to keep anyone from lying down. I have found a square of carpet by a gate that is not in use. My coat is my pillow and the announcements are my lullaby.

I have visited the care home every day for three weeks and today she did not know my name and I drove home anyway and here I am in the garage with the engine off. The door into the house is six feet away. I will open it in a minute.

The planting is done, four hundred seedlings, and my back will not straighten past a certain angle and I have stopped asking it to. I walk to the truck bent like a question mark. The water jug is empty and the sun is still up.

The toddler has been sick for five days and I have been awake for most of them and the pediatrician's hold music is the quietest thing I have heard all week. I sit on the bathroom floor with the phone on speaker. The tile is cool and I lie down on it.

The overnight bakery shift is done and the trays are washed and the sun is coming up as I walk home against the commuter traffic. Flour is in the creases of my knuckles. My bed is four blocks away and I am measuring them.

The inventory count is finished at two in the morning and every number on the clipboard has been checked twice and I no longer know what the numbers are for. The store lights hum. I sit on a pallet of dog food and look at the floor.

The deadline passed at midnight and the thing was sent and now it is one and I am sitting in front of the screen with nothing left to do and no idea how to stop. My hands are still on the keys. The cursor blinks at me in an empty document.

The potty training day ended with the seventh pair of pants in the wash and I am on the couch with the baby monitor and a glass of water I have not drunk. The television is on with the sound off. My eyelids have their own schedule.

The long drive back from the funeral ends in my own driveway at midnight and I sit there with the headlights on the garage door. The suit is wrinkled into me. I turn the key and the sudden quiet is almost too much to carry inside.

The sixth bedtime trip up the stairs and I am climbing them with my hand on the wall. He wants the door open a different amount. I adjust the door and sit on the top step in the dark and do not go down.

The harvest crew has gone and the combine is parked and I am in the kitchen with my boots off and my socks black with dust. The soup is on the stove and I do not get up to stir it. My arms rest on the table like things someone left there.

The last patient note is typed at eight and the clinic is dark and I am walking to the car through a lot that seems to have grown. My keys are heavier than keys. I get in and sit with the door open and one foot still on the pavement.

Mile three of the walk home with the dead phone and the broken-down car behind me and the shoes that were never meant for this. My heels are raw and I have stopped adjusting my stride around it. The streetlights go on one by one ahead of me and each one is farther than the last.

The envelope from the clinic is on the counter where I set it an hour ago and I have walked past it four times. It is thin, which could mean anything. My hands are cold and I keep them in my sleeves and do not pick it up.

The meeting invite arrived at four fifty on Friday with no agenda and two people from human resources on it, and it is Sunday night. I have reread the subject line until it means nothing. My stomach has been a fist since I saw it.

The vet's number is on the screen and the phone is ringing and I know what she is going to say about the bloodwork because of how she said tomorrow. I let it ring twice more. My thumb is over the green button and will not come down.

The exam hall doors are closed and we are lined up in the corridor and someone ahead of me is laughing too loud. My mouth is dry and the pencil case is slick in my hand. The doors will open in four minutes and I can feel each one of them.

The captain comes on and says we are going to hit some rough air and asks the crew to be seated, and the crew's faces do a thing. I tighten the belt that is already tight. The woman beside me puts her book down and we both look at the wing.

The hearing is at nine tomorrow and the suit is on the back of the door and I am lying on my back watching the ceiling fan go around. Every time I close my eyes the courtroom is there. The alarm is set and I will not need it.

The review is in thirty minutes and my manager has been in her office with the door shut since lunch, which she never does. I have opened and closed the same document six times. My coffee has gone cold and my hands have gone with it.
The drill whines from behind the door of the exam room and the chair I am waiting in faces that door. The receptionist smiles at me and I try to smile back. My tongue keeps finding the tooth.

The phone rings at three in the morning and the screen says my brother's name, and my brother does not call at three in the morning. I sit up and the room is very cold. I answer on the fourth ring because the first three were not possible.

The rumor has been going around since Monday and today the directors have been in the glass room all morning with the blinds down. People are typing without looking at their screens. I have a knot under my ribs that tightens each time the door opens.

The conference is at four and the teacher's email said she wanted to discuss some concerns, and the word concerns has been sitting in my chest all day. I park and do not get out. The hallway inside smells like it did when I was eight.

The results portal updates at noon and it is eleven fifty-two and the page is open on my phone and I have not refreshed it. The kitchen is very quiet. I pick up the phone and put it down and pick it up.

The examiner gets into the passenger seat with the clipboard and says pull out when you are ready, and I am not ready and the car is already in reverse. My foot is shaking on the brake. The parking lot has never looked so full of things to hit.

The attic hatch is open above me and the flashlight beam goes up into the dark and the noise has stopped, which is worse than when it was going. The ladder is cold under my hands. I put one foot on the first rung and wait there.

The letter from the tax office has the kind of window envelope that is never good news and it is addressed to me by my full legal name. I turn it over and over. The kitchen clock is loud and the letter stays sealed.

The nurse said the doctor would call back this afternoon and it is four thirty and the phone is on the table face up. Each time it buzzes with something else my whole body jumps and then settles into something heavier. I have not left the room.

The police tape is gone from the door and the locksmith has been and it is time to go back into the house. My key is in the lock and I have not turned it. Whatever they touched is still in there in the order they left it.

Tomorrow is the first day back after three months and the badge is on the counter and the laptop is charged and I have laid out clothes like a child. Everyone will ask how I am. I lie in the dark and rehearse a sentence I do not believe.

The knock comes at eleven at night, three slow knocks, and no one who knows us knocks like that. My husband and I look at each other across the living room. I am standing before I know I have stood and my legs are not sure about it.

The tech has gone quiet and is moving the wand back and forth over the same spot and the screen is turned away from me. The gel is cold on my stomach. I am watching her face because it is the only thing I can read.

The text says we need to talk and nothing else and she is not answering the follow-up. I am in the car outside the office with the engine running. The drive home is twenty minutes and I am not sure I want it to be shorter.

The dog's limp was better yesterday and worse this morning and the appointment is at two and he is lying by the door with his head on his paws. I sit on the floor next to him and do not look at the clock. My hand on his side is counting his breaths.

The warning light came on forty miles ago and the next town is sixty more and the engine has started making a sound underneath the radio. I turn the radio off. Every mile marker is a small victory I do not trust.

The tracks in the mud are fresh and wide and the claw marks are as long as my fingers and the trail goes exactly where they go. I stand still with my pack straps in both fists. The woods ahead have gone very quiet.

The ice ahead is a different color, grayer, with a line of open water beyond it, and the shore is behind me and the shortcut is in front. I slide one boot forward and the ice talks back. My breath has gone shallow and high in my chest.

The parking garage is empty at this hour and my car is on the fourth level and the elevator is out of order again. My footsteps come back to me off the concrete. I hold my keys between my fingers and do not run because running would mean something.

Surgery is at seven and it is five and I am sitting on the edge of the hospital bed in the gown with the strings that do not tie. The hallway outside is beginning to wake up. My hands are folded so they will stop doing other things.

I am third on the program and the second speaker is wrapping up and my slides are loaded and my throat has closed to a straw. The audience is four hundred dim shapes. I stand up before my name is called because sitting is worse.

The cruiser has been behind me for six blocks, matching my turns, and the registration expired last week and I know it. I keep both hands on the wheel and my eyes on the mirror more than the road. Any second now the lights will come on.
The bank's number is on the screen and the overdraft letter is beside the phone and I have to make this call before five. My thumb hovers. The hold music will be the easy part.

The school nurse left a message saying nothing was wrong but could I call, and nothing was wrong is a phrase that means something is. I am dialing from the car in the grocery lot. Each ring is longer than the one before.

The walk from my office to hers is forty steps and I am going to tell her the position is being eliminated and I have practiced the sentence and it is still the wrong sentence. Her door is open. I slow down for the last ten steps and it does not help.
The best man is standing and tapping his glass and I am next and the cards in my pocket are damp from my hand. Two hundred faces will turn. I take a sip of water that goes down the wrong way.

The forecast has the river cresting Thursday at a number two feet above the top of our sandbags and it is Tuesday night. I am standing at the back window watching water I cannot see yet. The pump is running and I keep listening for it to stop.

The basement lights are out and the breaker box is at the far end past the furnace and the flashlight is dimmer than it was last time. I go down three steps and stop. The dark down there has a shape and I am waiting for it to move.

The last contraction ended two minutes ago and the next one is coming, I can feel it building the way the last one did, and the last one was the worst so far. I grip the bed rail. The nurse says you are doing great and I do not believe her.
The proctor is walking down the rows with the booklets face down and she is two desks away. My pencils are lined up. My heart is going slow and hard like something knocking to be let out.

The coach is pinning the roster to the board and the whole team is pretending not to crowd toward it. I am at the back with my bag on my shoulder. The list is one sheet and my name is either on it or it is not and I cannot make my feet move.

The vet has taken the cat into the back and said she would be a few minutes and it has been twenty, and when it is nothing it is never twenty. The exam room has a poster about fleas. I read it for the fourth time.

The waiting room on the third floor has softer chairs than the others, and I know why, and I am sitting in one. My name will be called and a door will open and a man in a white coat will sit down slowly. I hold my coat in my lap like something that might get away.

The ladder flexes with every rung and the gutter is still four feet above me and the ground is a long way down and getting longer. I stop climbing. My hands are locked around the rails and I can feel my pulse in them.

The noise under the hood started as a tick and is now a knock and it is dark and the road has no shoulder. I turn the radio off to hear it better and wish I had not. The next exit sign says nineteen miles.

The school bus is three stops away and he is standing at the curb with the backpack that is bigger than his torso and I am holding his hand harder than he is holding mine. He has never been anywhere without me for six hours. My throat has something in it that will not go down.

The recital program has my daughter fourth and the third kid is halfway through and I am in the second row with my hands pressed between my knees. She looked at me once from the wings. I cannot play the piano for her and I want to.

The email went to the whole company instead of to Dan and I saw it a second after I hit send and the replies have not started yet. I am watching the inbox. Each new message that is not about it is a small reprieve I do not trust.

The test is on the bathroom counter and the timer on my phone says ninety seconds and I am sitting on the edge of the tub not looking at it. Either answer changes everything. My hands are between my knees and the fan is loud.

The lab portal is loading, the little wheel turning, and the result will be a number and I know which side of the line the number has to fall on. The wheel keeps turning. I have stopped breathing in a way I do not notice until my chest hurts.

The machine is a tube and the tech says it will take forty minutes and to hold still, and the table slides in with me on it. The ceiling is six inches from my face. The first bang comes and my whole body wants to be somewhere else.

The check-engine light is flashing, not steady, flashing, and the manual says that means pull over now and the shoulder is gravel on a curve. I am slowing down with the hazards on. The trucks behind me are not slowing down.

The principal's office is at the end of the hall and the secretary said he will see you now and I am an adult and my palms are sweating anyway. The hall is lined with children's drawings. I knock on the open door because my hand needs something to do.

The elevator is going down to the garage where my car is parked next to his, and his shift ends at the same time mine does, and the doors are closing. I press the button for the lobby instead and it does not light. The numbers go down one at a time.

The adoption agency said they would call by the end of the week with the committee's decision and it is Friday at four. My wife is at the window and I am at the table and neither of us is talking. The phone sits between us like a third person.

The smoke on the horizon has gone from a smudge to a wall since lunch and the evacuation map puts our road in the yellow band that touches the orange. The go bags are by the door. I keep walking to the window and the wall is closer each time.

The judge has gone back to chambers and the lawyers are whispering and I am on the bench with my hands clamped between my knees. The clock above the door has no second hand. When the side door opens I will know from her face.

The biopsy was Monday and they said a week and it is Friday and every time the phone rings I know, and then it is my mother, and then it is a survey. I have stopped answering with hello. The weekend is a hallway with no doors.

The climbing rope is rigged and the edge of the cliff is three feet away and below it is nothing for a hundred feet, and it is my turn to lean back into the harness. My knees have gone to water. The instructor says I have you and the words do not reach my hands.

I take the 7:40 bus from the stop at the end of my street. It runs down the avenue for eleven stops and turns left at the hospital. I get off at the stop after the library and walk two blocks north to the office.

The kitchen has four upper cabinets and three lower ones. I keep the plates in the cabinet to the left of the sink and the glasses above the dishwasher. Pots and pans are in the drawer under the oven.

The library I use has three floors. Fiction is on the ground floor along the east wall, nonfiction is on the second floor, and the periodicals and the study rooms are on the third. The elevator is next to the main stairs.
I park on the second level of the garage, in the row nearest the stairwell. The garage has five levels and the exit ramp spirals down on the north side. The ticket machine takes cards and coins.
I sort the laundry into three piles: whites, darks, and towels. The whites go in on hot with the long cycle and the darks go in on cold. Towels run separately and go in the dryer for sixty minutes.

I rinse one cup of rice until the water runs mostly clear. It goes in the pot with one and a half cups of water and a pinch of salt. I bring it to a boil, cover it, and turn the heat to low for eighteen minutes.

The hardware store where I shop has plumbing in aisle three and electrical in aisle four. Paint is at the back by the mixing counter, and fasteners are in the bins along the left wall. The garden section is outside through the side door.
The timetable at my stop lists departures every fifteen minutes between six and nine in the morning. After nine they run every half hour until seven at night. On Sundays the first bus is at eight.
My desk is on the third floor near the window that faces the parking lot. The printer is around the corner by the supply closet. The kitchen is at the far end of the floor past the conference rooms.

The forecast I read for tomorrow shows a high of fifty-four and a low of thirty-eight. Winds are from the northwest at ten to fifteen miles an hour. There is a thirty percent chance of rain after four in the afternoon.

I measure the room from wall to wall with the tape. It is twelve feet four inches by ten feet ten inches, with the closet door on the north wall. The window is thirty-six inches wide and sits forty inches from the floor.
The map shows the trail starting at the lot and following the creek for a mile and a half. At the fork I take the left branch, which climbs to the overlook. The loop returns along the service road.

I count the boxes on the shelf and write the numbers on the sheet. There are fourteen of the small size, nine of the medium, and three of the large. The sheet goes in the folder on the manager's desk.

I turn the pot on its side and slide the plant out with the root ball intact. The new pot is two inches wider and has a layer of gravel in the bottom. I fill around the roots with soil and water it until the tray collects runoff.

The mail has three envelopes, a catalog, and a flyer from the grocery store. The envelopes are a bill from the water company, a statement from the bank, and a card addressed to my daughter. I put the flyer and the catalog in the recycling.

The dishwasher's normal cycle runs two hours and ten minutes. I load the plates in the bottom rack facing the center and the glasses along the sides of the top rack. The detergent goes in the compartment on the inside of the door.

I ride the bike path along the river for four miles to the second bridge. From there I cross over and take the street with the bike lane into downtown. The ride takes about twenty-five minutes each way.
The update window says the download is one point two gigabytes. I click install and the laptop restarts twice. The whole process takes about twenty minutes and ends at the login screen.

The pickup line forms along the fence on the south side of the school. I enter from the side street and pull forward to the cones. A teacher with a clipboard reads the number on my dashboard card and calls the child out.
The bank opens at nine. I take a number from the dispenser by the door and sit in the row of chairs facing the tellers. When my number appears on the screen I go to window three.
I plug the printer into the wall and connect the cable to the back of the computer. The setup program finds it and asks for a name. I load the tray with letter paper and print a test page.

The list is in the order of the store: produce first, then bread, then dairy along the back wall. The canned goods are in the middle aisles and the frozen section is last. I write the quantities in the margin.

My trash is collected on Tuesdays and recycling every other Friday. I put the bins at the curb the night before with the handles facing the house. Yard waste is picked up on the first Monday of the month from April to November.
My apartment has two bedrooms off a central hallway. The bathroom is between them and the kitchen opens onto the living room at the front. The door to the balcony is on the west wall.

The dashboard of my car shows the speedometer in the center with the fuel gauge on the right. The odometer reads eighty-four thousand two hundred miles. I set the trip counter to zero at the start of each tank.

I unscrew the cap on the front tire and press the gauge onto the valve. It reads thirty-two pounds and the door sticker says thirty-five. I add air at the station pump in short bursts and check it again.
I have the thermostat set to sixty-eight from six in the morning until ten at night. At ten it drops to sixty-two until six. On weekends the daytime setting starts at seven.
The spreadsheet has columns for the date, the vendor, the amount, and the category. Each row is one receipt. The total at the bottom updates when I enter a new line.
The dog eats one cup of dry food at seven in the morning and another at six at night. His water bowl is refilled when I feed him. The bag of food is kept in the bin by the back door.
I water the front beds on Mondays and Thursdays before eight. The hose reaches the far corner if I use the second spigot. Each bed gets about ten minutes with the sprinkler head on the fan setting.
I take the red line six stops to the transfer station. The green line platform is one level down and the trains run every eight minutes. From the last stop it is a five-minute walk to the building.

The museum I visit has the permanent collection on the first and second floors and the temporary exhibits on the third. The coat check is to the left of the entrance and the cafe is in the basement. Admission is free on the first Sunday of each month.

The shelf comes in a flat box with two side panels, four shelves, and a back panel. I attach the shelves to one side with the long screws, then the other side, then nail the back panel on. The whole assembly takes about forty minutes.
My mailbox is at the end of the driveway on the right side. The carrier comes between one and two in the afternoon on weekdays. Packages that do not fit are left on the porch by the door.
The elevator has buttons for the basement, the lobby, and floors two through nine. My office is on seven. The doors close after about five seconds and the ride from the lobby takes under a minute.
I give the pharmacist my name and date of birth at the pickup counter. She scans the bag and asks whether I have questions about the dosage. I pay at the register and sign on the pad.

I put six eggs in a pot and cover them with cold water by an inch. When the water boils I turn off the heat and set a timer for eleven minutes. Then I move the eggs to a bowl of ice water for five minutes.
The recycling center I drive to has separate bins for glass, cardboard, and metal. Electronics go in the trailer at the back of the lot. The attendant checks the sticker on my windshield at the gate.

The appointment is at two thirty on the fourth floor of the medical building. Parking is in the lot behind the building and the entrance faces the street. I bring the insurance card and the list of medications.
I renew the bus pass at the kiosk in the station. The screen asks for the card number and the number of months. The pass loads onto the card after the payment goes through.

I run the thread from the spool through the guide at the top, down through the tension discs, and up through the take-up lever. Then it comes down to the needle and through the eye from front to back. The bobbin sits in the case under the plate.
The oil is due every five thousand miles or six months, whichever comes first. The sticker on the windshield gives the next date and mileage. I schedule it at the shop on the corner.
I check in at the kiosk and scan my passport. The machine prints a boarding pass and a bag tag. I drop the bag at the counter and go through security to gate twenty-two.

The commuter lot I use has two hundred spaces and fills by eight on weekdays. The shuttle to the station leaves from the shelter at the north end every ten minutes. I buy a daily permit for four dollars at the machine.

I check in at the front desk and give the name on the reservation. The clerk hands me two key cards and says the room is on the fifth floor. Breakfast is served in the room off the lobby from six to ten.
I arrange the books by author's last name across the four shelves. Reference books are on the bottom shelf and the paperbacks are on top. The dictionary stays on the desk.
I set up the board with the white square in the corner on my right. The rooks go in the corners, then the knights, then the bishops. The queen goes on her own color and the king next to her.

The court where I play is seventy-eight feet long and thirty-six feet wide for doubles. The net is three feet high at the center. The service boxes are twenty-one feet deep and the baseline is marked with white tape.
My garden has four raised beds, each four feet by eight. Tomatoes are in the bed nearest the fence and beans are in the one beside it. The two beds by the shed have lettuce and herbs.
The compost bin takes vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, and eggshells. Meat and dairy go in the trash. I turn the pile with a fork once a week and add leaves from the pile behind the garage.

I lock the bike to the rack outside the station with the U-lock through the frame and the front wheel. The cable goes through the back wheel and the seat rails. The key goes on the ring with the house keys.
The printer I use takes letter paper in the main tray and legal in the side tray. Envelopes feed through the slot on the front. The toner cartridge is behind the panel on the right side.
I open the stapler and remove the empty strip. The new staples go in with the points facing down. I close the top and press it once on a scrap of paper to seat them.
Monday has a meeting at ten and a dentist appointment at three. Tuesday and Wednesday are open except for the call at nine. Thursday I am out of the office and Friday has the review at two.
The mail route covers the six streets between the river and the rail line. I start at the north end and work south, then come back up the other side. The route takes about four hours on foot.

The ferry I take leaves the mainland on the hour from seven in the morning to nine at night. The crossing takes thirty-five minutes. Cars board from the lower ramp and foot passengers from the upper deck.

On my street, residents with a permit may park on the east side. The west side is two-hour parking from eight to six. Street cleaning is on the second Wednesday of the month and both sides must be clear.
I put paper and cardboard in the blue bin and glass and cans in the green bin. The black bin is for everything else. The bins are picked up from the alley behind the building.
My drawer to the left of the stove has the spatulas, the whisk, and the tongs. The drawer below it has the dish towels. The measuring cups hang on hooks inside the cabinet door.

The drive to the airport takes forty minutes without traffic. I take the parkway north to the exit for the terminal road and follow the signs for departures. The long-term lot is on the left before the terminal loop.
The rain gauge on the fence post shows three quarters of an inch since yesterday morning. I write the number in the notebook with the date. The gauge gets emptied each time I record it.

The water meter is in the box by the sidewalk under a metal lid. The dial reads in cubic feet and the small needle counts tenths. I read it on the first of the month and enter the number on the utility's website.
My router has four lights on the front. The first is power, the second is the internet connection, and the third and fourth are the two wireless bands. The reset button is a small hole on the back.
My water heater is in the closet off the garage. The dial on the front is set to the middle position, which the label says is one hundred twenty degrees. The shutoff valve is on the pipe above it.
The tide table I check lists low tide at six twelve in the morning and high tide at twelve forty. The second low is at six thirty in the evening. The heights are given in feet above the chart datum.
The sign at my stop lists the three routes that serve it and the hours they run. The number of the stop is printed at the bottom for the text service. A bench and a shelter are on the sidewalk side.

I go to the polling place at the elementary school on the corner. The poll worker checks my name against the list and hands me a ballot. I fill it out in the booth and feed it into the scanner by the door.
The library card application asks for a photo identification and proof of address. The card is printed at the desk while I wait. It allows twenty items at a time for three weeks each.

Each entry in the lab notebook starts with the date and the experiment number. I write the materials on the left page and the procedure on the right. Results go below the procedure with the page initialed at the bottom.
I pull into the car wash and put the car in neutral when the light turns green. The track pulls the car through the brushes and the rinse arch. At the end the dryers run for about thirty seconds.

The washing machine has settings for normal, delicate, and heavy. The water temperature dial has cold, warm, and hot. I use normal and cold for most loads and add the detergent to the drawer on the left.
I insert the card and enter the four-digit code. The screen offers withdrawal, deposit, and balance. I select withdrawal, choose the amount, and take the cash and the card from the slots.

The campus map I carry shows the science building at the north end of the quad and the library at the south. The student center is on the east side next to the parking structure. Lecture halls are numbered by building and floor.
The pool where I swim has six lanes. Lanes one and two are for slow swimmers, three and four for medium, and five and six for fast. Lap swim runs from six to eight in the morning on weekdays.

The piano gets tuned twice a year, in the spring and the fall. The tuner comes to the house and the visit takes about ninety minutes. I move the lamp and the photographs off the top before he arrives.
The haircut is at eleven on Saturday at the shop on the main street. I park in the lot behind the row of stores. The cut takes about twenty minutes and I pay at the counter by the door.

I mix three cups of flour, one teaspoon of salt, and one packet of yeast in the bowl. I add one and a quarter cups of water and stir until the dough comes together. It rests under a towel for an hour before shaping.
The seed packet I bought says to plant a half inch deep and six inches apart after the last frost. Germination takes seven to ten days. The plants reach maturity in about sixty days.
I wear a size ten in running shoes and a nine and a half in dress shoes. The boots are an eleven because I wear thick socks with them. The sizes are written on a card in my wallet.
The bus from the airport makes nine stops before the central station. I get off at the seventh, which is the stop for the university. The ride takes about thirty-five minutes in the evening.
My sock drawer is the top drawer on the left. Black socks are in the front and white socks in the back. The wool socks are in a separate box on the closet shelf.
The kitchen fixture takes two sixty-watt equivalent bulbs. The hallway sconces take candelabra bulbs at forty watts. I keep spares of each in the box on the top shelf of the pantry.

The label on the paint can I bought lists the color name and number on the top. The coverage is given as four hundred square feet per gallon. Drying time to the touch is one hour and recoat time is four.
My phone has one hundred twenty-eight gigabytes of storage and ninety-one are in use. Photos take up the largest share at forty gigabytes. The settings screen lists each application and its size.
I back up the laptop to the external drive on the first of each month. The program copies the documents folder and the photos folder. The drive is kept in the desk drawer between backups.
The train I take to the city leaves from platform four. The express stops at three stations and the local stops at eleven. The schedule is posted on the board above the ticket windows.
The receipt lists milk, eggs, bread, two pounds of apples, and a bag of rice. The subtotal is twenty-three dollars and the tax is one dollar and forty cents. I paid with the debit card.

The weather station on my roof records temperature, humidity, and wind speed every ten minutes. The readings go to a display in the kitchen. The rainfall sensor is a tipping bucket that counts hundredths of an inch.
The recipe serves four and I am making it for eight. I double the flour and the butter and the eggs. The baking time stays the same but I use two pans instead of one.
My hallway closet holds the vacuum, the ironing board, and the winter coats. The top shelf has the extra blankets and the box of light bulbs. The broom hangs on a hook inside the door.
The shelves in my garage are set at eighteen-inch intervals. The bottom shelf holds the paint cans and the middle shelves hold the bins of tools. The top shelf is for the camping gear.
My living room window measures sixty inches wide by forty-eight inches tall. The sill is thirty inches from the floor. The curtain rod is mounted six inches above the frame.
My garage has the car on the left side and the workbench along the back wall. The lawnmower and the bikes are on the right. The recycling bins are by the door into the house.
I take the stairs to the fourth floor and turn right at the top. The office is the third door on the left, past the water fountain. The sign on the door lists the hours as nine to five.
